Angle Bisector

GeometryConstructionsTriangles
Game: Move the two sides of an angle and watch a line that always sits exactly halfway between them.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Drag D along the side or R to change the circles, then press Check the claims.
Look for the math

An angle can be split exactly in half with just a circle and a pair of equal circles. The line you get turns out to be much more than a way to cut the angle: it is the path of every point that is equally far from the two sides.

Copy the length to the other ray

Start with the corner A and two rays through B and C. Pick D on the first ray, then draw the dotted circle centred at A through D. Its crossing with the other ray is E, so AD = AE. This is Euclid's step (I.9), and it is why E sits on the same ray as C rather than behind A.

Two equal circles make a common chord

Now draw two circles of the same radius, centred at D and E. Drag R to change that radius together for both. Their two crossings are P and F, and the line through them is the perpendicular bisector of DE. Because AD = AE, that line passes through A. Because DF = EF, the triangles ADF and AEF have three matching sides, so they are congruent. The two angles at A match, and AF is the angle bisector. The applet picks F, the crossing farther from A. When its drawn bisector is more than three pixels off, the applet draws the common chord itself instead — the same line, found a surer way.

Equally far from both sides

Drop a perpendicular from F to each ray. Triangle ADF has base AD and triangle AEF has base AE; those bases are equal and the triangles are congruent, so their areas match and the two heights — the distances from F to the rays — match too: dist(F, AB) = dist(F, AC). The same argument works for every point on the line, which is what makes the bisector a locus of points equally far from the two lines. The logic test checks this at F and at four more points on the line, over hundreds of angles. Drag B or C yourself and press Check the claims to see the two distances stay equal.

Euclid's special radius, and the real minimum

Euclid made DEF equilateral, which means the common radius is DE; press Use DE (Euclid) to see it. The article says a radius greater than AD is a sure choice, and the test confirms that. It is sure, but not the smallest possible: the circles first touch at DE/2 = AD·sin(A/2), which is always less than AD for an angle below 180°. Shrink R past that bound and F disappears.

Try dragging R inward until the two circles just kiss, then press Use DE (Euclid) and watch F jump outward again.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
